A.q: Which quadrant has tasks that are Not Urgent and Important?
options: Quadrant 1
Quadrant 2
Quadrant 3
Quadrant 4
A.explain: Quadrant 2 = Not Urgent + Important: planning, prevention, preparation.

A.q: What does 'urgent' mean?
options: Tasks that you can safely postpone to any later time
Tasks connected only to your distant long-term goals
Tasks that demand your immediate attention right NOW
Tasks that serve your mission, values, and priorities
A.explain: Urgent means it requires attention NOW.

A.q: Which term means judging each task by its worth and its deadline?
options: Scheduling
Planning
Priorities
Organization
A.explain: Priorities = a value judgment on each task by its worth and its deadline.

A.q: Which of the following is known as the enemy of time management?
options: Setting goals
Procrastination
Prioritizing tasks
Self-evaluation
A.explain: Procrastination is the enemy of time management.

A.q: Which statement best defines time management?
options: Completing as many separate tasks as you possibly can in a single day without any planning at all
Developing the processes and tools that increase your efficiency and productivity
Spending every single available hour of the entire week purely on academic work
Avoiding all of the activities that seem to require your immediate attention today
A.explain: Time management = developing processes and tools that increase efficiency and productivity.

A.q: Which statement best distinguishes an urgent activity from an important activity?
options: Urgent activities tend to feel enjoyable, whereas important activities always feel quite difficult and demanding
Urgent activities are always important, while important activities are never ever urgent in any way
Urgent activities need immediate attention; important activities serve your mission, values, and priorities
Urgent activities are distant long-term goals, while important activities are mere daily interruptions
A.explain: Urgent = immediate attention (a timing claim); important = contributes to priorities and values (a mission claim).

A.q: A critical assignment due today greatly affects a student's progress. Which quadrant?
options: Quadrant I: Urgent and Important
Quadrant IV: Not Urgent and Not Important
Quadrant III: Urgent and Not Important
Quadrant II: Not Urgent and Important
A.explain: Due today = urgent; major effect on progress = important → Quadrant I.

A.q: Which activity is the best example of Quadrant II: Not Urgent and Important?
options: Playing games during scheduled study time
Responding to a crisis that requires immediate action
Planning a study schedule before examinations begin
Answering an unimportant interruption immediately
A.explain: Planning before exams is important but not pressing today, making it the classic Quadrant II activity.

A.q: Why is Quadrant II called the heart of personal quality management?
options: It consists mainly of entertainment and pure time-wasting activities with no real value
It lets people comfortably avoid all of their everyday responsibilities entirely
It holds every single urgent crisis that has to be solved right now immediately
It centers on planning, capacity building, prevention, and preparation
A.explain: Quadrant II focuses on planning, capacity development, prevention, and preparation.

A.q: What is likely to happen when a person consistently neglects Quadrant II activities?
options: Every single task on the list will become less important
The person will manage to eliminate all interruptions permanently
The person will no longer have any need to prioritize tasks
Important activities may drift into Quadrant I as urgent crises
A.explain: Neglected QII items get promoted into Quadrant I as urgent crises.

A.q: Which is the most appropriate first priority when several tasks compete for attention?
options: The task carrying the greatest value and the nearest deadline
The very task that your instructor happened to assign to you most recently of all
The easiest task to finish, regardless of how important it is
The task that you personally find the most enjoyable to do
A.explain: First priority = greatest value + nearest deadline.

A.q: Which combination represents the three key steps to good time management?
options: Hourly meetings, continuous messaging, and task avoidance
Daily exercise, social media review, and spontaneous planning
Weekly schedule, daily to-do-list, and long-term planning
Crisis response, multitasking, and delaying difficult tasks
A.explain: Weekly schedule + daily to-do list + long-term planning.

A.q: What is the primary purpose of developing a weekly schedule?
options: To completely replace any need for daily planning or lists
To make sure that every single minute is spent working
To give an overview of your committed time and free time
To keep a record of only the tasks left unfinished
A.explain: A weekly schedule shows committed time against available time.

A.q: What behavior is an early warning sign of time-management problems?
options: Frequently asking teachers for extensions
Using a long-term plan to organize future work
Completing important tasks before their deadlines
Preparing a weekly schedule in advance
A.explain: Regularly asking for extensions is an early warning sign.

A.q: What is likely a consequence of procrastinating on an important academic task?
options: More sleep and improved learning
Increased anxiety and poorer-quality work
Lower stress without any disadvantages
More time for completing the task carefully
A.explain: Procrastination → increased anxiety and poorer-quality work.

A.q: Which task belongs in Quadrant III: Urgent and Not Important?
options: Carefully preparing your overall long-term academic study strategy for the whole term
Finishing a high-stakes critical assignment that is due today
An interruption needing attention now but serving no real priority
Casually playing a game when no deadline or benefit exists
A.explain: QIII = urgent but does not support major priorities, the classic interruption.

A.q: Which activity is the clearest example of Quadrant IV: Not Urgent and Not Important?
options: Preventing future academic problems through careful forward planning
Completing a high-value critical task that is due today
Responding promptly to a serious and unexpected emergency
Spending study time on games and unnecessary chatting
A.explain: Games and unnecessary chatting = neither deadline nor payoff = QIV.

A.q: Which outcome is a direct benefit of effective time management?
options: A firm guarantee that no urgent task will ever occur again
Less anxiety because of better preparation and clear prioritization
The rare ability to finish absolutely all tasks at once
The total and complete elimination of every single one of your daily responsibilities
A.explain: Better preparation and prioritization reduce anxiety.

A.q: A student wants to spend more time on important activities and reduce last-minute crises. Which strategy is best?
options: Concentrate mainly on interruptions simply because they feel immediate
Schedule important activities early and review them each week
Delay starting any task until it finally becomes urgent
Wait until inner motivation arrives before touching important work
A.explain: Plan important activities early and review them weekly, a deliberate QII investment.

A.q: Which statement best defines Time Management?
options: An inborn natural talent that only a fortunate few people are simply ever born with
The total number of hours that a single dedicated student spends studying each week
A clever and highly systematic method of dodging every single urgent and pressing task
The development of processes and tools that increase efficiency and productivity
A.explain: TM = development of processes and tools that increase efficiency and productivity.

A.q: Time management is also defined as the ability to:
options: Work on the tasks that you personally enjoy the most each day
Get things done when they should be done
Memorize the entire college timetable by heart
Avoid deadlines by carefully renegotiating them each time
A.explain: Get things done when they should be done: right task, right time.

A.q: How does time management develop?
options: It is a skill requiring steady work, a lifelong challenge for most
It simply happens on its own as a person grows older
It can be learned once early on and then forgotten forever
It stays permanently and totally fixed at exactly the same level for every single person
A.explain: It is a skill that must be worked on, a life-long challenge for most people.

A.q: In the matrix, 'urgent' activities are those requiring:
options: Careful long-term planning
Permission from a supervisor
Immediate attention (NOW)
A written budget first
A.explain: Urgent = immediate attention (NOW).

A.q: In the matrix, 'important' activities are those that:
options: Tend to be the loudest and the most visible of all the daily tasks
Always appear right at the very top of your crowded and busy inbox
Can safely be handed off and delegated to just about anyone around
Contribute to your mission, your values, and your priorities
A.explain: Important = contributes to your mission, values, and priorities.

A.q: If an activity is urgent, does that automatically mean it is important?
options: Yes, because a task being urgent proves that it is equally important
It does, provided a teacher personally assigned that particular task
No, an urgent activity can still contribute nothing to your mission
It does, during the busy weeks when formal examinations are being held
A.explain: No, urgency is a timing claim; importance is a mission claim.

A.q: Which items belong to Quadrant I (Urgent & Important)?
options: Trivia, busy work, distractions, and time wasters such as chatting and pointless idle daily games
Crisis, pressing problems, and deadline-driven projects critical to your strategic priorities
Interruptions, some calls, some mails, some reports, some meetings, and many popular activities
Chatting, games, excessive TV, and other not-urgent not-important time-wasting daily pastimes
A.explain: QI: crisis, pressing problems, deadline-driven projects critical to strategic priorities.

A.q: Which items belong to Quadrant II (Not urgent & Important)?
options: Preventing problems, strategy planning, relationship building, and recognizing new opportunities
Reacting to sudden crises, working long deadline-driven all-nighters, and constant daily firefighting
Fielding nonstop interruptions, taking some calls, and dealing with every single pressing matter
Indulging in trivia, busy work, distractions, and pointless chatting and games daily time wasters
A.explain: QII: prevention, anticipation, strategy planning, relationship building, new opportunities.

A.q: Which items belong to Quadrant III (Urgent & Not important)?
options: Interruptions, some calls, some mails, some reports, some meetings, and pressing matters
Preventing problems, strategy planning, relationship building, and recognizing opportunities
Crisis, pressing problems, and deadline-driven projects critical to your strategic priorities
Trivia, busy work, distractions, and time wasters such as chatting and games and excessive TV
A.explain: QIII: interruptions, some calls/mails/reports/meetings, pressing matters.

A.q: Which items belong to Quadrant IV (Not urgent & Not important)?
options: Confronting sudden crises and other pressing important problems head-on
Investing steady time in careful relationship-building activities
Trivia, busy work, distractions, and wasters like chat and games
Putting real effort into preventing your future important problems
A.explain: QIV: trivia, busy work, distractions, time wasters (chatting and games).

A.q: Which quadrant is called 'the heart of the personal quality management'?
options: Quadrant I: Urgent & Important
Quadrant II: Not urgent & Important
Quadrant III: Urgent & Not important
Quadrant IV: Not urgent & Not important
A.explain: Quadrant II is 'the heart of the personal quality management'.

A.q: To lead effectively, you need to spend more time in:
options: Quadrant I: personally handling every crisis
Quadrant II: important but not urgent work
Quadrant III: answering every interruption
Quadrant IV: recovering from the week
A.explain: Spend more time in Quadrant II, the Important but not Urgent quadrant.

A.q: What happens when you do not spend enough time in Quadrant II?
options: Your personal mission and your core values change all by themselves automatically
Many items move over into Quadrant I, and you are constantly handling crises
All of the Quadrant IV distraction items simply disappear forever on their own
Each and every one of your daily work tasks suddenly becomes thoroughly enjoyable
A.explain: Items move into Quadrant I and you are constantly handling crises.

A.q: Which is a real benefit of good time management?
options: It promises you top grades in every course without any effort
It wipes out absolutely every single source of stress in life
It readies you for life's demands, which in turn lowers anxiety
It magically shortens the length of the academic semester for you
A.explain: Better prepared for life's demands → decreases anxiety.

A.q: Good time management helps you assign time to tasks:
options: Equally across all tasks, regardless of their size (Equalizing)
In the order in which the tasks arrive, one after another (Sequencing)
In proportion to each task's true importance (Prioritizing)
According to how enjoyable or fun each task is (Favoring)
A.explain: Assign time in proportion to each task's true importance (Prioritizing).

A.q: Which of the following is listed as an early warning sign of time management problems?
options: Finishing every single assigned task well before its deadline
Keeping a tidy weekly schedule
Asking teachers for extensions regularly
Sleeping eight hours a night
A.explain: Asking teachers for extensions regularly is on the warning-sign list.

A.q: 'Your grades don't reflect your ability' is an example of:
options: Listed as an early warning sign of time management problems
Offered as proof that the recent examinations were simply unfair
Framed as a clear reason to change your major immediately
Stated as a fixed rule about the nature of intelligence
A.explain: It is an early warning sign: the remedy starts with completing the Time Management Matrix.

A.q: Procrastination may give immediate satisfaction, but it brings:
options: Anxiety, reduced sleep, illness, lower grades, poorer work, rushed learning, and disappointment
Sharper and much deeper learning that comes from intense last-minute focused cramming sessions
Considerably more free relaxation time paired with markedly higher-quality finished academic work
Markedly stronger and far warmer personal relationships with all of your course instructors
A.explain: The full bill: anxiety, reduced sleep, illness, lower grades, poorer work, less learning, disappointment.

A.q: Setting priorities means making a value judgment on each task based on:
options: Judged mainly by its overall length and its level of difficulty
Decided by whatever particular mood you happen to be in that day
Sorted strictly according to the alphabetical order of the task name
Weighed by its true worth and by when it must be completed
A.explain: Worth and when it must be completed.

A.q: Which tasks should be your #1 priority?
options: The handful of tasks that you personally enjoy doing the most
The very easiest tasks, chosen mainly to build early momentum
The tasks that are worth the most and that are due soonest
The same tasks that most of your friends happen to be doing
A.explain: Worth the most + due the soonest = #1 priority.

A.q: Which of the following are the three key steps to good time management?
options: Depending entirely on last-minute cramming, brief napping, and plain repetition
Making a weekly schedule, a daily to-do list, and a long-term plan
Forcing yourself to work harder, sleep much less, and skip meals
Repeating nothing but memorizing, thick highlighting, and endless rereading
A.explain: Weekly schedule, daily to-do list, long-term plan.

A.q: What is the purpose of developing a weekly schedule?
options: To give a clear overview of your free and your committed time
To keep a careful record of the grades from every single quiz
To maintain a tidy list of the phone numbers of classmates
To track exactly how much of your pocket money is being spent
A.explain: An overview of free and committed time.

A.q: A call demands attention now but serves no mission or value. Which quadrant?
options: Quadrant I
Quadrant II
Quadrant III
Quadrant IV
A.explain: Some calls and interruptions = urgent but not important = QIII.

A.q: You plan next term's strategy and build a study partnership; nothing is due. Which quadrant?
options: Quadrant I
Quadrant II
Quadrant III
Quadrant IV
A.explain: Strategy planning + relationship building, no deadline = QII.

A.q: Two hours disappear into trivia, busy work, and chatting-and-games time wasters. Which quadrant absorbed the time?
options: Quadrant I
Quadrant II
Quadrant III
Quadrant IV
A.explain: Trivia, busy work, chatting and games = QIV.

A.q: A 42-hour week includes 21 hours of urgent and important work. What share is that?
A.explain: 21 of 42 hours = 50% in Quadrant I.

A.q: After listing your weekly tasks in the Urgent & Important matrix, what should you do next?
options: Keep the completed matrix hidden away from all of your close and trusted colleagues
Put the first things first, then share and discuss with the colleague beside you
Cross out and delete every single task that you previously placed in the Quadrant I
Rewrite the whole filled-in matrix later on as a formal and structured written essay
A.explain: Put first things first, then share and discuss with the colleague beside you.

A.q: What is the purpose of writing a daily to-do list?
options: To provide daily reminders to assure that key tasks are not forgotten
To sort and rank all of your classmates carefully by their latest exam grades
To take over and completely replace the need for a careful weekly schedule
To keep a private daily record of all your dreams and your shifting moods
A.explain: Daily reminders so key tasks are not forgotten.

A.q: What is the purpose of preparing a long-term plan?
options: Commit to memory all the key dates needed for a single history exam
Step in to fully replace the daily to-do list for every given day
Allow you to dodge and avoid ever stopping to plan out the week
To promote your overall organization and careful future planning
A.explain: Promotes overall organization and future planning.

A.q: Time management is best described as a skill that:
options: a motivated person can pick up quickly and then set aside
improves on its own as a person gains more years of experience
everyone must keep working on it in every area of their life
depends on a person's natural talent rather than on steady practice
A.explain: Everyone must work on it in all areas: personal, academic, and work. It is a lifelong skill, not picked up once, not automatic with age, and not based on natural talent.

A.q: Successful time management requires:
options: Expensive specialist software and a quiet private office of your own
Permission from the dean
Self-evaluation and the desire to improve
A lighter course load
A.explain: Self-evaluation and the desire to improve.

A.q: Effective time management will ultimately require a person to:
options: Make yourself do unwanted tasks at times you would rather not
Just wait for inner motivation to arrive on its own
Confine your effort to studying the subjects you already like best
Steer clear of and politely avoid every one of your unpleasant daily tasks
A.explain: Do things you don't want to do when you don't want to do them, and push yourself; the pay-off is always worth the effort.

A.q: Which early warning sign of TM problems involves the quality of submitted work?
options: Turning in submitted work that falls below your own usual standard
Making a point of attending each and every lecture right on time
Wrapping up and finishing all of your assigned tasks well early
Recording and keeping every single commitment neatly inside a calendar
A.explain: Submitting work below your usual standard is a listed warning sign.

A.q: Which warning sign involves sacrificing things you like?
options: Setting aside quiet hours each weekend purely for reading for pleasure and light fiction
Choosing to join and regularly attend a weekly peer study group with others together
Deciding to settle down and go to sleep early the night before exams well in advance
Having to let go of activities you enjoy because of a lack of time or low grades
A.explain: Letting go of activities you enjoy due to lack of time or low grades is a warning sign.

A.q: Urgent activities can take us away from:
options: The very activities that let us carry out our mission or our vision
Our nightly sleep and our three daily meals, and little else
Our leisure time spent scrolling social media feeds and playing casual video games
Nothing, as urgency itself is seldom a true problem
A.explain: Urgent activities steal time from mission- and vision-carrying activities.

A.q: By definition, procrastination is:
options: It is best understood as a completely harmless and innocent little habit
It is viewed as a clever and modern evidence-based study technique
It is described plainly as the true enemy of good time management
It is celebrated wrongly as the essential secret key to real creativity
A.explain: 'Procrastination: Enemy of Time Management.'

A.q: Good time management ultimately makes a person:
options: A far more productive and successful person who enjoys a balanced life
A person left isolated and cut off from all friends and family
Someone wholly dependent on your instructor for every single decision made
An individual rendered completely immune to and unaffected by any deadline
A.explain: A more productive, successful person with a more balanced life.

A.q: Match each quadrant to the activities the matrix places in it.

rightItems.text: Crisis, pressing problems, deadline projects, and meetings
Prevention, planning, relationship building, and personal development
Interruptions, some calls, some mails, and popular activities
Trivia, some phone calls, excessive TV, and games

A.explain: Quadrant I holds crises, pressing problems, deadline projects and meetings; Quadrant II holds prevention, planning, relationships and personal development; Quadrant III holds interruptions, some calls and mails and popular activities; Quadrant IV holds trivia, some phone calls, excessive TV and games.

A.q: Match each quadrant to the result of living in it.

rightItems.text: Stress, burnout, and always putting out fires
Vision, perspective, balance, control, and few crises
Short-term focus and feeling victimized and out of control
Irresponsibility, work not completed, and loss of your job

A.explain: Living in Quadrant I brings stress and burnout; Quadrant II brings vision, balance and control; Quadrant III brings short-term focus and feeling victimized; Quadrant IV brings irresponsibility and loss of your job.

A.q: Match each key step to its purpose.

rightItems.text: Gives an overview of free and committed time
Provides reminders so key tasks are not forgotten
Promotes overall organization and future foresight

A.explain: The weekly schedule gives an overview of free and committed time; the daily to-do list provides reminders so key tasks are not forgotten; the long-term plan promotes overall organization and future foresight.

A.q: A student wants to define and develop this study skill.

steps.prompt: It is the development of processes and what else?
options: tools
rules
budgets
uniforms

steps.prompt: These processes and tools mainly increase efficiency and what?
options: productivity
popularity
proximity
parity

steps.prompt: Because efficiency and productivity need steady work, time management is a what?
options: a lifelong challenge
a one-time quick fix
an inborn natural talent
a fixed permanent trait

A.explain: Step 1: time management develops processes and tools. Step 2: these raise efficiency and productivity. Step 3: it is a skill worked on continuously, a lifelong challenge for most, not a one-time fix, inborn talent, or fixed trait.

A.q: The matrix sorts every task along two axes.

steps.prompt: The axis that demands attention NOW is called what?
options: urgency
importance
priority
vision

steps.prompt: Urgency is a timing claim; the other axis, importance, is a claim about what?
options: your mission and values
your inbox order
your mood today
your budget

steps.prompt: Since importance is a mission claim, can an urgent task fail to be important?
options: yes, because urgency does not prove importance
no, because the two labels mean the same thing
it depends on who assigned the task
it depends on the exam calendar

A.explain: Step 1: the NOW axis is urgency. Step 2: importance is a mission and values claim, not inbox, mood, or budget. Step 3: because importance is a mission claim, an urgent task can be unimportant; the two labels are not identical and do not depend on who assigned it or the calendar.

A.q: Which of the following are among the seven key practices of Quadrant II?
options: Improving communication with others
Better planning and organization
Watching excessive TV and games
Constantly putting out fires
A.explain: Improving communication and better planning are Quadrant II practices. Watching excessive TV is a Quadrant IV time waster, and constantly putting out fires is a Quadrant I result, not a practice.

A.q: Which is named as the key practice of Quadrant II?
options: Knowing what is important
Doing better preparation each term
Looking after and caring for yourself
Pursuing ongoing personal development
A.explain: Knowing what is important is the key practice. Better preparation, caring for yourself, and personal development are also Quadrant II practices, but the slide names knowing what is important as the key one.

A.q: Which are listed as Quadrant II practices?
options: Taking advantage of new opportunities
Caring for yourself
Fielding some mails and calls
Reacting to pressing problems
A.explain: Taking advantage of new opportunities and caring for yourself are Quadrant II practices. Fielding some mails and calls is Quadrant III, and reacting to pressing problems is Quadrant I.

A.q: Living in Quadrant IV most likely leads to what?
options: Irresponsibility and loss of your job
Vision, balance, and control
Stress and burnout
Feeling victimized and out of control
A.explain: Living in Quadrant IV brings irresponsibility, work not completed, and loss of your job. Vision and balance come from Quadrant II, stress and burnout from Quadrant I, and feeling victimized from Quadrant III.

A.q: Which is NOT one of the seven Quadrant II practices?
options: Improving communication with others
Better preparation
Handling every crisis personally
Personal development
A.explain: Handling every crisis personally is not a Quadrant II practice; it reflects living in Quadrant I. Improving communication, better preparation, and personal development are all listed practices.

A.q: Good time management helps a student do what?
options: Get the most out of their education
Avoid every single academic responsibility they hold
Skip long-term planning entirely
Rely fully on the instructor
A.explain: Time management helps you get the most out of your education. It does not let you avoid responsibilities, skip planning, or rely fully on an instructor.

A.q: Which early warning sign means work is turned in after its due time?
options: Handing work in late
Forgetting commitments
Making excuses for undone work
Submitting below-standard work
A.explain: Handing work in late is a warning sign about timing. Forgetting commitments, making excuses, and submitting below-standard work are also warning signs, but the timing one is handing work in late.

A.q: Forgetting what you promised to do is an early warning sign of what?
options: time management problems
practicing effective leadership skills
Quadrant II planning
procrastination relief
A.explain: Forgetting commitments is an early warning sign of time management problems. It is not a mark of effective leadership, Quadrant II planning, or relief from procrastination.

A.q: Often lacking enough time to finish a task signals what?
options: a time management problem
a deeply balanced and calm life
strong future planning
low anxiety levels
A.explain: Often not having enough time to complete a task signals a time management problem, not a balanced life, strong planning, or low anxiety.

A.q: Offering reasons for why work was not done is a warning sign of what?
options: time management problems
good prioritizing habits
effective weekly schedules
clear personal values
A.explain: Making excuses for why work is not done is a warning sign of time management problems, not a sign of good prioritizing, effective schedules, or clear values.

A.q: What should you complete to gauge how much you need this skill?
options: the Time Management Matrix
a single daily to-do list
the college timetable
a long-term budget plan
A.explain: You should take time to complete the Time Management Matrix to see how much you need to work on this skill. A daily list, the timetable, or a budget plan does not measure it.

A.q: In the end, procrastination does what relative to helping you?
options: hurts you more than it helps
helps you more than it hurts
neither truly helps nor really hurts you at all
its help outweighs any harm
A.explain: In the end procrastination hurts you more than it helps you. It does not help more than hurt, is not neutral, and its help does not outweigh the harm.

A.q: At any one time you may ideally have how many tasks to do?
A.explain: You may have about 10 tasks you ideally should work on, and it is impossible to do them all. One, two, or a hundred are not the number described.

A.q: The pay-off of good time management is said to be what?
options: always worth the effort
rarely worth the effort
a reward reserved for managers
a reward reserved for students
A.explain: The pay-off of good time management is always worth the effort. It is not rarely worth it, nor a reward reserved for managers or for students alone.

A.q: After sharing your matrix, the next step is to do what?
options: discuss what each could do differently
carefully hide the matrix from all colleagues
delete every Quadrant I task
rewrite the matrix as an essay
A.explain: The third step is to discuss together what each person could do differently to do more important activities. Hiding the matrix, deleting Quadrant I tasks, or rewriting it as an essay are not part of it.

A.q: In the simple banner matrix, which item is listed under Quadrant I?
options: Meetings
Preparation
Interruptions
Trivia
A.explain: The banner matrix lists meetings under Quadrant I with crises and deadlines. Preparation is Quadrant II, interruptions Quadrant III, and trivia Quadrant IV.

A.q: Match each quadrant to the Urgent and Important combination that defines it.
A.explain: Quadrant I pairs with Urgent and Important; Quadrant II with Not urgent and Important; Quadrant III with Urgent and Not important; Quadrant IV with Not urgent and Not important.
